title: How much does one AI-generated game prop actually cost?
author: LevelUsual1367
selftext:
I'm working on a small Unity project and needed an old handheld radio as a prop. Nothing fancy, but players can pick it up and inspect it, so the knobs and smaller details need to look decent up close.

I started looking into Meshy and figured the 100 free credits a month would be enough to experiment. Then I got curious about how much I'd actually be spending on each usable asset.

The Pro plan is $20 for 1,000 credits, which works out to about $0.02 per credit if you use the whole allowance.

Going by the current rates, a Meshy 7 model costs around $0.50 to generate, and adding textures is another $0.20. So roughly $0.70 for a textured model. Not bad, until you need three attempts because the antenna keeps looking weird. Now you're at $2.10 for one prop, before touching anything in Blender.

The free plan is a little different. You can generate models with the monthly credits, but that doesn't mean every model is free to download. Free downloads are limited to eligible Lite models, and commercial use of free-plan assets requires attribution under CC BY 4.0. API access is paid too.

The part I'm still figuring out is whether a subscription makes sense for my workflow. If I'm making assets regularly, $20 a month seems pretty reasonable. But if I only need one radio, it's not really a $0.70 purchase when I have to pay for the subscription.

And that's before counting the time spent fixing geometry or getting everything ready for Unity.

How do you guys budget for AI-generated assets? Do you count all the failed attempts and cleanup time, or just the generation cost?

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body:
Any assets generated by AI are not copyrightable, so they have no basis for requiring attribution. They can't tell you how you're allowed to use assets that no one owns.

ETA, since all the replies seem to have skipped reading the OP: The context here is the license Meshy claims to hold over its output, and my point is that they have no right to try to enforce a license on output they don't own.

comments.author: pornhonked
comments.body: I’ve built several hundred models using procedural generation in Opus 5.5, and the result for a real-time strategy game was acceptable. You can easily identify all of the assets. Claude ran a recursive process with another agent checking its work, all based upon publicly available photos. It was quite expensive though, it took 6 or so hours for \~70 Chinese vehicles. I then switched to Meshy as a test for a couple of higher fidelity assets, aiming for 100,000 polygons for an F-35. The result is a more realistic model, but if you look closely, you can easily tell that it’s been generated from a photo by Meshy. I still haven’t found an AI solution that provides high fidelity game models (of real-world military vehicles) that look good up close. If anyone has any suggestions, please share

comments.author: ImpressiveGooseHead
comments.body:
Im a skilled modeler, and generally I’m using Meshy to get to basically what a scanned asset reference would give you.

In other words, it’s unusable as-is, but it’ll fast forward the concept and initial blockout phases a lot.

From there if it’s easy to model, or needs super clean hard surfaces, like a radio? Just sculpt by hand, using the generated asset as scale reference. 

If it’s organic like a character, then I’d use meshys low poly as a starter for that and clean up from there.

comments.author: SignificanceLanky988
comments.body:
I'd definitely count failed attempts and cleanup time. Generation cost alone gets pretty misleading once you care about the final usable asset.

I've actually been working on a free/open-source tool called Construct that takes a different approach to this. Instead of generating the final mesh directly, the agent builds the object from named parts, so something like a radio can keep its knobs, switches, antenna, etc. as actual separate parts. I have a tape recorder example that's pretty close to what you're describing.

For simple props I've had good results using cheap models like DeepSeek, so the actual model cost can be very low. Complex stuff is a completely different story though — cars with multiple critic/revision rounds can get expensive fast.

I'd probably measure cost per *accepted* asset rather than per generation: failed attempts + revisions + cleanup + human time. A $0.70 generation isn't really $0.70 if you need three tries and half an hour in Blender.

Construct is here if you want to try the radio with it: [https://github.com/rtmandreyev/construct](https://github.com/rtmandreyev/construct)

It's free, so at least you can compare the approach without buying another subscription.

comments.author: Furyan9x
comments.body:
I haven't started on assets yet since I'm still in the early stages, so I love finding posts like this so I can learn from you guys lol

I have a bunch of research done and lined up spike tests to trial run different pipelines, I'm eager to see the results of those.

comments.author: Spoonman915
comments.body:
I'm not sure if meshy has a generation option that will create quads, but if so, that is the way to go. A lot of time the default model generators on the AI sites create meshes that are better for sculpting, imho. 

I use tripo, so things will be different obvs. But I posted my first video on my youtube and it's about getting quad meshes out of tripo. I run the process on a character, but the same concepts apply to hard surface. using 3 or 4 views and the multiview feature to generate the mesh. I would just maybe do a pass in blender or something with aI telling it to go in and add sharp edges in blender where the angle is >X. 

You'd probably want to do something to eliminate unecessary polys as well, as the minimum on Tripo smart mesh is 500, which seems like overkill for a knob. Whatever AI you use, I would definitely split it out into parts and use something like smartmesh to generate it though. Could also retopo the triangulated meshes in blender. qremesher or quadrify is also an option.

Here's the link to the vid if you're interested.  
[https://youtu.be/cq5afY6qB6I](https://youtu.be/cq5afY6qB6I)
